stem: I said to my friend, "Can I borrow your dictionary for one day?"
optA: I asked my friend if I could borrow his dictionary for one day.
optB: I asked my friend if I could borrow your dictionary for one day.
optC: I asked my friend if I can borrow his dictionary for one day
optD: I asked my friend that if I can borrow his dictionary for one day.
solution: An interrogative is reported with 'asked ... if' and no 'that'. 'Can' backshifts to 'could', and the second-person 'your' (addressed to the friend) becomes 'his'. Option B keeps 'your', C keeps 'can', and D wrongly adds 'that' before 'if'. Matches option A.

stem: He said, "Let Hari come with us, mother. I'll take care of him"
optA: He requested his mother to let Hari come with them as he will take care of him.
optB: He informed his mother to let Hari come with them as he would take care of him.
optC: He told his mother to let Hari come with them as he would take care of him.
optD: He told to his mother let Hari come with us as he would take care of him.
solution: The imperative 'Let Hari come' is reported with 'told ... to let'. 'Us' becomes 'them' and 'I'll' backshifts to 'would'. Option A fails to backshift ('will'), B misuses 'informed ... to', and D says 'told to his mother' and keeps 'us'. Matches option C.

stem: "No," said the child, "I won't kneel, for if I do, I shall spoil my new pair of trousers."
optA: The child said that he would not kneel for if he did so he will spoil his new pair of trousers.
optB: The child said that he will not kneel for if he kneels he will spoil his new pair of trousers.
optC: The child said that he would not kneel for if he did so he would spoil his new pair of trousers.
optD: The child said that I will not kneel for if he did kneel, he should spoil his new pair of trousers.
solution: Both 'won't' and 'shall' backshift to 'would', and the present 'do' becomes 'did'. Option A leaves the second verb as 'will', B backshifts nothing, and D keeps the first-person 'I'. Matches option C.

stem: The chairman of the selection committee said, "We shall finalise the rest of our team after we have selected the skipper."
optA: The chairman of the selection committee told that they would finalise the rest of our team after we have selected the skipper.
optB: The chairman of the selection committee said that we would finalise the rest of our team after we have selected the skipper
optC: The chairman of the selection committee said that they would finalise the rest of their team after they selected the skipper.
optD: The chairman of the selection committee said that they would finalise the rest of their team after they had selected the skipper.
solution: 'We/our' become 'they/their', 'shall' becomes 'would', and the present perfect 'have selected' backshifts to the past perfect 'had selected'. Option C uses only the simple past, A and B fail to convert the pronouns. Matches option D.

stem: He said, "Has anybody been unkind to you ?"
optA: He asked me if anybody had been unkind to me.
optB: He asked me had anybody been unkind to me.
optC: He asked me if anybody had been unkind to you.
optD: He asked me if anybody had been unkind to him.
solution: A yes/no question is reported with 'asked ... if' in statement order, so 'has been' backshifts to 'had been' and the 'you' addressed to the speaker's listener becomes 'me'. Option B keeps the interrogative order, C keeps 'you', D wrongly shifts to 'him'. Matches option A.

stem: The pilot said, "Please don't panic but tighten your seat belts."
optA: The pilot told to the passengers that they should not panic but tighten the seat belts
optB: The pilot told the passengers to not panic but to tighten their seat belts instead.
optC: The pilot told the passengers not to panic but to tighten your seat belts
optD: The pilot told the passengers not to panic but to tighten their seat belts.
solution: A negative imperative is reported as 'told ... not to'. 'Your' becomes 'their'. Option A says 'told to the passengers', B splits the infinitive and adds an unwarranted 'instead', and C keeps 'your'. Matches option D.

stem: He said, "Ravi, why are you sounding so depressed today?"
optA: He asked Ravi why did he sound so depressed that day.
optB: He asked Ravi why he was sounding so depressed that day.
optC: He told Ravi why he sounded so depressed today.
optD: He asked Ravi that why was he sounding so depressed that day.
solution: A wh-question is reported with 'asked' plus statement word order, so 'are you sounding' becomes 'he was sounding' and 'today' becomes 'that day'. Options A and D keep the interrogative inversion, C uses 'told' and keeps 'today'. Matches option B.
reviewNote: DUP of bank row bfe17d83-655b-45d7-9e2e-bd8615436758 (identical stem, identical options in the same order, same key B). Stays PRIVATE.

stem: "I shall remain here and the tailor won't be able to find me," said she.
optA: She said that she should remain there and the tailor won't be able to find me.
optB: She said that she should remain there and the tailor would not be able to find her.
optC: She said that she would remain there and the tailor would not be able to find her.
optD: She said that, she could remain here and the tailor would not find her.
solution: First-person 'shall' backshifts to 'would' (not 'should', which would change the meaning to obligation), 'won't' to 'would not', 'here' to 'there' and 'me' to 'her'. Matches option C.

stem: Mother said, "Gaurav, you will be eligible for voting when you are 18."
optA: Mother told Gaurav he would be eligible for voting when he was 18
optB: Mother told Gaurav that he could vote only after 18.
optC: Mother told Gaurav you will be eligible for voting when you are 18.
optD: Mother told Gaurav that he would be eligible for voting when he would be 18.
solution: 'Will' backshifts to 'would' in the main clause and 'are' to 'was' in the time clause. Option D wrongly puts 'would' inside the 'when' clause, C makes no change at all, and B rewrites the sense rather than reporting it. Matches option A.

stem: He said, "Bravo ! You have done well."
optA: He applauded him to say that he had done well.
optB: He applauded him and said that you have done well.
optC: He applauded him, saying that he has done well.
optD: He applauded him, saying that he had done well.
solution: The exclamation 'Bravo!' is reported by the reporting verb 'applauded', and the present perfect 'have done' backshifts to 'had done'. Option A misuses 'to say', B keeps 'you have', and C fails to backshift. Matches option D.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: ANIMOSITY
solution: Animosity is strong hostility or ill will, so its opposite is affection or love. 'Lust', 'luck' and 'loss' are unrelated. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: ALTERCATION
solution: An altercation is a noisy quarrel or dispute; a compromise is the settling of a dispute, hence its opposite. 'Challenge' and 'opposition' are closer to synonyms. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: COAX
solution: To coax is to persuade someone gently to do something; to dissuade is to persuade them not to. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: ERUDITE
solution: Erudite means having or showing great learning, so 'unscholarly' is the opposite. 'Educated' and 'scholarly' are synonyms and act as traps. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: AFFLUENT
solution: Affluent means wealthy, so its opposite is poor. 'Fluent' is a sound-alike trap. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: PAROCHIAL
solution: Parochial means narrow or restricted in outlook, confined to one's own locality, so 'narrow' is a synonym trap. The natural axis of opposition is local versus global, which makes 'global' the best antonym. Matches option C.
reviewNote: FLAWED but keyed to the OFFICIAL LWS key (C). The defect is that option D 'world wide' is an exact synonym of the keyed option C 'global', and option B 'international' is also a defensible antonym, so three of the four options oppose PAROCHIAL and two of them are indistinguishable. Held PRIVATE so it never enters the browsable bank; the official key is preserved verbatim so OMR grading matches how the students were graded.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: FALLIBLE
solution: Fallible means liable to err or capable of making mistakes; 'unerring' means never making a mistake, the precise opposite. 'Reliable' and 'trustful' concern trustworthiness rather than freedom from error, and 'falsehood' is a noun. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Related to bank row 59c8b76b (antonym of 'fallible' keyed 'perfect') but a distinct item — disjoint option set and a different answer word. Kept new per the Dinner-3 DILIGENT precedent.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: IMPERTINENT
solution: Impertinent means rude or not showing proper respect, so 'respectful' is the direct opposite. 'Arrogance' is a noun and a near-synonym in sense, while 'modest' opposes boastfulness rather than rudeness. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Resolved: keyed C on the dominant modern sense (insolent), and the official LWS key confirms C. Option B 'appropriate' would be defensible only under the older sense 'not pertinent'.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: ROUGH
solution: In its primary sense rough describes an uneven surface, whose direct opposite is smooth. 'Refined' and 'polite' oppose only the secondary sense of coarse manners. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Resolved: keyed C on the primary (texture) sense, and the official LWS key confirms C. 'Refined' and 'polite' would be defensible only for the secondary 'coarse manners' sense.

stem: Choose the word which is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word given: RATIFICATION
solution: Ratification is formal approval or confirmation, so 'disapproval' is its opposite and the only option that is both a noun and semantically opposed. 'Disagreeable' and 'disturbing' are adjectives, and 'denial' opposes assertion rather than approval. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: The failure of crops in successive years put the farmer \(\underline{\text{in a tight corner}}\).
solution: 'In a tight corner' means in a difficult or awkward predicament from which escape is hard. The other options read the phrase literally. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: The effort to trace the culprit was \(\underline{\text{a wild goose chase}}\).
solution: A wild goose chase is a hopeless pursuit of something unattainable, hence a futile search. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: The story does not \(\underline{\text{hold water}}\).
solution: If an account does not hold water it fails to stand up to scrutiny, that is, it cannot be believed. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: Raj couldn't pay the bill, so he asked the owner to \(\underline{\text{put it on the cuff}}\).
solution: 'On the cuff' means on credit, from the old practice of a barman chalking a debt on his shirt cuff. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: His statement is \(\underline{\text{out and out}}\) a lie.
solution: 'Out and out' means completely or thoroughly, so it intensifies rather than qualifies. 'Merely' and 'slightly' weaken the claim. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: The luxury car that they bought turned out to be \(\underline{\text{a white elephant}}\).
solution: A white elephant is a possession that costs more to keep than it is worth. 'Turned out to be' signals disappointment, ruling out the positive options. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: If you are \(\underline{\text{fair and square}}\) in your work you will definitely prosper.
solution: 'Fair and square' means in an honest and straightforward manner. Matches option B.
reviewNote: DUP of bank row dfdcea82-2ad3-4003-b10e-9d563d8ef98a (same idiom, key 'in an honest way'). Stays PRIVATE.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: There is \(\underline{\text{no love lost}}\) between any two neighbouring countries in the world.
solution: 'No love lost between X and Y' means they dislike each other, that is, they are not on good terms. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: The heavy downpour \(\underline{\text{played havoc}}\) in the coastal area.
solution: To play havoc is to cause widespread destruction or devastation. The other options name possible side effects rather than the meaning of the idiom. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase in bold: To have \(\underline{\text{a green thumb}}\) means
optC: to have a natural interest in gardening
optD: one has a green tattoo on the thumb
solution: 'To have a green thumb' (British: green fingers) means to have a natural talent for and interest in growing plants. Options A and D read it literally. Matches option C.

context: In an effort to produce the largest, fastest and most luxurious ship afloat, the British built the S.S. Titanic. It was so superior to anything else on the seas that it was dubbed 'unsinkable'. So sure of this were the owners that they provided only twenty life boats and rafts, less than one-half the number needed for the 2,227 passengers on board. Many passengers were aboard the night it rammed an iceberg only two days at sea and more than halfway between England and its New-York destination. Because the luxury liner was travelling so fast, it was impossible to avoid the ghostly looking iceberg. An unextinguished fire also contributed to the ship's submersion. Panic increased the number of casualties as people jumped into the icy water or fought to be among the few to board the life boats. Four hours after the mishap, another ship, the 'Carpathia', rescued 705 survivors. The infamous S. S. Titanic had enjoyed only two days of sailing glory on its maiden voyage in 1912 before plunging into 12,000 feet of water near the coast of Newfoundland where it lies today.
stem: All of the following are true except that
optA: Only a third of those aboard perished
optC: The S.S. Titanic sank near Newfoundland
optD: The S.S. Titanic was the fastest ship afloat in 1912
solution: The passage gives 2,227 passengers on board and 705 survivors, so roughly two-thirds perished and only about a third survived. Statement A reverses this and is therefore the false one. The Carpathia rescue, the Newfoundland location and the claim that the ship was the fastest afloat are all stated in the passage. Matches option A.

stem: All of the following contributed to the large death toll except
solution: The passage names panic, an unextinguished fire and the liner's speed as contributors to the disaster. The Carpathia arrived four hours later and rescued 705 survivors, so it reduced the death toll rather than adding to it. Matches option D.

stem: How many days was the S.S. Titanic at sea before sinking ?
solution: The passage states the ship rammed the iceberg 'only two days at sea' and that it 'had enjoyed only two days of sailing glory'. The 4 is the hours before rescue and the 12 belongs to the 12,000 feet of water. Matches option A.

stem: Maiden voyage is closest in meaning to
solution: A maiden voyage is a ship's first journey, so 'inaugural' is closest in meaning. The passage supports this: the ship sank on this voyage in 1912 after only two days. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Related to bank row 8a7e69fa ('maiden appearance' keyed 'first') but a distinct item — different context, option set and question class (in-passage vocabulary vs standalone synonym). Kept new.

stem: What does this passage convey?
optA: The S.S. Titanic proved itself the most seaworthy vessel in 1912
optB: Attempts to rescue the S.S. Titanic's survivors were not successful
optC: Overconfidence by builders and owners was greatly responsible for the sinking of the vessel
optD: A fire and panic were the only causes for the sinking of the ship
solution: The passage stresses that the ship was dubbed 'unsinkable' and that the owners were 'so sure of this' that they carried less than half the lifeboats needed, which points to overconfidence as the underlying cause. A is contradicted by the sinking, B by the rescue of 705 survivors, and D by the word 'only' since speed and the iceberg also contributed. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the one word which can be substituted for the given words/sentence: A person who opposes war or use of military force
solution: A pacifist believes that war and violence are unjustifiable. A fascist favours authoritarian nationalism, a narcissist is excessively self-admiring, and a fatalist believes events are predetermined. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the one word which can be substituted for the given words/sentence: Severely abusive writing in journals
solution: Scurrilous writing makes scandalous and abusive claims about someone. 'Sarcastic' implies mockery rather than abuse, and the other two concern invention rather than insult. Matches option C.

stem: Choose the one word which can be substituted for the given words/sentence: Call upon God or any other power (like law) etc. for help or protection
solution: Invocation is the act of calling on a deity or authority for aid. Involution is complexity or inward curling, inundation is flooding, and revocation is cancellation. Matches option A.

stem: Choose the one word which can be substituted for the given words/sentence: Fear of being enclosed in a small closed space
solution: Claustrophobia is the fear of confined spaces. Agoraphobia is its opposite, the fear of open or public places; xenophobia is fear of foreigners; paranoia is unfounded suspicion. Matches option B.

stem: Choose the one word which can be substituted for the given words/sentence: One who has become dependent on something or drugs is
solution: An addict is a person dependent on a substance or habit. 'Adamant' means unyielding, an 'edict' is an official order, and 'derelict' means abandoned or neglectful. Matches option C.

stem: Select the alternative which best expresses the same sentence in Active Voice: He was congratulated by his teacher on his brilliant success in the recent examination.
optA: His teacher congratulated him on his brilliant success in the recent examination.
optB: His teacher congratulated him for his success in the examination.
optC: His teacher congratulated him on his success.
solution: Converting to the active voice makes the agent 'his teacher' the subject and 'him' the object, while every other element of the sentence must be retained. Options B, C and D drop information from the original. Matches option A.

stem: Select the alternative which best expresses the same sentence in Passive Voice: People speak English all over the world.
optA: English is spoken all over the world.
optB: English was spoken all over the world.
solution: The simple present active becomes 'is spoken' in the passive, and the vague agent 'people' is normally dropped while the adverbial 'all over the world' is kept. Options B and C wrongly shift to the past, and D drops the adverbial. Matches option A.

stem: Select the alternative which best expresses the same sentence in Passive Voice: Who gave you permission to enter?
optA: By whom were you given permission to enter?
optB: By whom was you given permission to enter?
optC: By whom you were given permission to enter?
optD: By whom given you permission to enter?
solution: 'Who' becomes 'By whom' in the passive, and the subject 'you' takes the plural-form verb 'were'. Option B uses 'was' with 'you', C drops the interrogative inversion, and D omits the auxiliary. Matches option A.

stem: Select the alternative which best expresses the same sentence in Passive Voice: The Principal has granted him a scholarship.
optA: A scholarship has granted to him by the Principal.
optB: He has been granted a scholarship by the Principal.
optC: He has granted a scholarship by the Principal.
optD: A scholarship was granted to him by the Principal.
solution: The present perfect active 'has granted' becomes 'has been granted' in the passive. Options A and C omit 'been', and D shifts the tense to the simple past. Matches option B.

stem: Select the alternative which best expresses the same sentence in Active Voice: Before festivals the shops are thronged with men, women and children making various purchases.
optA: During festivals people throng the shops.
optB: Men, women and children throng the shops before festivals making various purchases.
optC: Men, women and children make purchases during festivals
optD: The shops are througed by people making purchases.
solution: In the active voice the agent 'men, women and children' becomes the subject and 'the shops' the object, with 'before festivals' and 'making various purchases' retained. Options A and C change 'before' to 'during' and drop detail, and D remains passive. Matches option B.

stem: Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence: (1) The lead story / (P) at 4 AM / (Q) in tonight's news / (R) concerns the fire / (S) which engulfed the Columbia College / (6) this morning.
solution: The prepositional phrase Q 'in tonight's news' must modify the opening subject 'The lead story', then R supplies its verb 'concerns the fire', S is the relative clause describing that fire, and P 'at 4 AM' joins the closing 'this morning' to give the time. The order is QRSP. Matches option B.

stem: Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence: (1) In less than a week / (P) the processor controlled exchange / (Q) have restored the functioning of / (R) which had suffered / (S) the telecommunication people / (6) a major disaster.
solution: The plural subject S 'the telecommunication people' takes the plural verb Q 'have restored the functioning of', whose object is P 'the processor controlled exchange'; R 'which had suffered' then leads into the closing 'a major disaster'. The order is SQPR. Matches option D.

stem: Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence: (1) As my jogging-enthusiast sister / (P) was often bothered by neighbourhood dogs / (Q) with a stick in hand, / (R) her husband started to accompany her on a bicycle, / (S) on her daily run, / (6) to ward off any attackers.
solution: The subordinate clause needs its verb first, so P follows the opening, then S 'on her daily run' completes it. The main clause R states what the husband did, and Q 'with a stick in hand' leads naturally into the closing purpose 'to ward off any attackers'. The order is PSRQ. Matches option B.

stem: Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence: (1) An electrical circuit / (P) which is / (Q) of wires / (R) designed to / (S) is a circle / (6) carry electricity.
solution: The subject needs its verb S 'is a circle', which Q 'of wires' then qualifies; the relative clause P 'which is' plus R 'designed to' leads into the closing 'carry electricity'. The order is SQPR. Matches option A.

stem: Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence: (1) We have pleasure / (P) a double room with bath / (Q) for five days from September 4 to September 8, / (R) that we have reserved / (S) in informing you / (6) both days inclusive.
solution: The idiom is 'have pleasure in informing you', so S follows the opening; R 'that we have reserved' introduces the reported content, P names what was reserved, and Q gives the dates leading into the closing 'both days inclusive'. The order is SRPQ. Matches option B.
